english: would you like to come for dinner?

terms.gloss: you’ll dine at my house: come to dinner
terms.grammar: future of cēnō, with apud mē (apud nōs), and the guest’s name in the vocative
evidence: Catull. 13.1: cēnābis bene, mī Fabulle, apud mē
Mart. 11.52.1: cēnābis bellē, Jūlī Ceriālis, apud mē
Plaut. Curc. 728: tū, mīles, apud mē cēnābis
terms.comment: The invitation as the poets make it: not a question but a friendly future, “you’ll dine at mine”. Martial adds condiciō est melior sī tibi nūlla, venī, “if you have no better offer, come”, and Cicero writes to his brother cēnābis cum vēneris. To ask, use vīn': Plautus’s guest asks vīn' ad tē ad cēnam veniam?, “shall I come to yours for dinner?” (see “come”). For the verb “invite”, see “invite”.

phrases.latin: cēnābis bene, mī Fabulle, apud mē paucīs, sī tibi dī favent, diēbus
phrases.english: you’ll dine well at my house, my Fabullus, in a few days, if the gods are kind to you

phrases.latin: cēnābis bellē, Jūlī Ceriālis, apud mē; condiciō est melior sī tibi nūlla, venī. octāvam poteris servāre; lavābimur ūnā
phrases.english: you’ll dine nicely at my house, Julius Cerialis; if you have no better offer, come. You can keep to the eighth hour; we’ll go to the baths together

phrases.latin: Sī potes Archiacīs convīva recumbere lectīs nec modicā cēnāre timēs holus omne patellā, suprēmō tē sōle domī, Torquāte, manēbō.
phrases.english: If you can bear to recline as my guest on plain couches, and are not afraid to dine on nothing but greens from a modest dish, I’ll expect you at my house at sunset, Torquatus.

phrases.latin: Mē ad cēnam vocā. — Pol vērō vocō. — Eāmus intrō hinc. — Fīat.
phrases.english: Invite me to dinner. — I do indeed. — Let’s go in, then. — Right.

phrases.latin: Vīn' crās apud nōs cēnāre? — Libenter, sī vacābō.
phrases.english: Would you like to come for dinner tomorrow? — I’d love to, if I’m free.

sources: Lewis & Short: ceno · Lewis & Short: apud
